newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-WOODS ADDS TO LEGEND, WINS DISNEY WORLD CLASSIC.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-WOODS ADDS TO LEGEND, WINS DISNEY WORLD CLASSIC.

text.p: Despite a bad cold which left him weak dizzy and miserable, Tiger Woods added another amazing chapter to his storybook start as a pro by winning the Disney World event Sunday over Payne Stewart.
The 20-year-old Woods finished at 21 under par after a round of six-under 66 which included three three-putt bogeys.

He finished one shot ahead of former U.S. Open and PGA champion Stewart, although he had seemed headed for a playoff against Taylor Smith, before his fellow-rookie was disqualified for using a putter with non-conforming grips.
The one-shot victory was Woods's second in his last three events, and came in just his seventh start as a professional.
Asked about his phenomenal success, Woods replied: "It might be surprising to you, but not to the people who know me. I haven't played my best golf yet.
"I've been hitting it good, but not great, and haven't had a great putting round yet. I have managed my game really well."
The win and the $216,000 first-place check brings Woods up to 23rd place on the 1996 money list with an incredible $734,794, and puts him 14th on the Ryder Cup points list.
Woods finished with the same score as Smith, 29. Smith, a co-leader as the round began, shot 67 to get to 21 under which would have forced a playoff, but was disqualified.
Smith uses a 44-inch split grip putter, and USGA rules state that a putter with two separate grips must have grips which are perfectly round -- Smith's are oval shaped and are flattened on one side.
Smith was paired with Lennie Clements, who is one of the few players on the PGA Tour to use a split grip putter, and Clements noticed that Smith's grips were non-conforming.

Clements reported it to rules officials, and Smith was told at the turn he was disqualified. At the time Smith was a stroke behind Woods, and refused to accept disqualification. He asked to play the rest of the round and then appeal.
Said Smith, "I didn't care if I didn't make a penny this week, I wanted to get to 22 under par, so that I would know that I won the tournament."
Instead, Smith sank a three-footer for birdie on the 18th hole to finish at 21 under, and will always wonder whether or not he could have beaten Woods in sudden death and won.
Said Woods, "I have mixed emotions. I feel like I should have been in a playoff. I feel bad for Taylor because he played his heart out."

The Disney Classic was the last full field event of the 1996 season. Woods's move to 23rd place dropped Lee Janzen out of the top 30 who qualified to compete for $3 million next week in the Tour Championship at Southern Hills.
"Tiger is the greatest thing that's happened to the tour in a long time," said an admiring Stewart, whose 67 was not quite enough on Sunday.
"He has brought incredible attention to golf at a time of year when football and the World Series always take precedence. Everything I've heard about him seems to be true."
Woods continued to produce spectacular results. In the 27 rounds Woods has played as a pro he is 95 strokes under par for a remarkable stroke average of 67.89.

"What you guys don't understand is that when I was playing before (in pro events) I was a teenager, I was in high school and in college," said the 20-year-old Woods, who stormed into golf's spotlight by winning three successive U.S. Amateurs.
"I had term papers and exams, and I was playing in the majors, the toughest tournaments in the world," the former Stanford University student said.
"I never was able to get into a rhythm to play. Now that I'm out here full time, just look at my finishes - 60th, 11th, fifth, third, first, third, first. It's kind of a good rhythm."
